story_text.value:
Hi folks, This is Vicky, I build privacy focused tools and utilities with Local AI on late nights and weekends.

I came here to talk about my new product Smart Blur - Smart Build Labs, a Chrome/Browser extension that blurs sensitive things on any web page before anyone else sees them. There are already quite a few options available that does the same. So why new one? Two reasons 1. Open AI Local Model: Existing product uses regex to find email, phone, ssn etc. But these do not understand the context and doesn't work on unstructured PII like Names and Addresses. Smart Blur uses WebGPU to run the local model directly on machine and detect PII before it gets leaked 2. Share Shield that auto detects the screen sharing from browser and turn on your blur mode. This is a life saving feature for those whose life runs on demos and meetings. It also automatically turns off the blur as soon as sharing stops.

Please give it try. No account and no server needed. The product has been designed to keep privacy in mind.

story_text.value:
For quite some time, this was my routine. I'd wake up and grab my phone before I was even properly awake, scrolling Slack, YouTube, LinkedIn and X. Then I'd sit on the toilet scrolling through half-open eyes. My brain would scream to get rid of it, but somehow I couldn't. By the end, I felt groggy, my legs hurt, my eyes were burning, and I felt tired & like shit. I tried to avoid using my phone right after waking up, but there was always some reason to pick up the phone, and then the whole thing just kept on repeating. Then one morning I left my phone at home and went out for a walk and to buy some groceries (I still have a habit of carrying cash with me). It was the best I'd felt in quite some time. That's when I realised the phone had to stay out of my mornings. I couldn't find a blocker that kicks in the moment you wake up, so I built one.

It's called AM Buffer. You set your alarms in the app and pick which apps to block. When the alarm goes off, those apps stay locked for as long as you choose. One feature came from testing it on myself. I woke up a bit early one morning to check that the alarm worked, and before it even rang I'd drifted back into scrolling. A lot of people wake up a little before their alarm, so the premium paid version now starts blocking an hour before your first alarm too (along with some other features). These days my mornings feel a bit calmer. I spend that time with my wife, doing house stuff or just chilling.

It's on TestFlight now, iPhone only, iOS 26 and up. The first three mornings unlock everything for free, including the pre-alarm blocking.

I'm the developer, and I'd really like to know three things:

- Is this actually useful to you, or does willpower already do the job? - Would you pay for it, and what feels fair? - What should I build next?

Some of the features that I am already planning to build are: - A group feature for some social accountability angle. - Personal streaks & group streaks.

story_text.value:
Dependency-free POSIX compatibility layer and build environment for UEFI.

https://gitlab.com/bztsrc/posix-uefi

Its goal is twofold: provides the usual libc API for EFI applications and an SDK on POSIX systems to create such EFI applications with a build system that works with CLang and gcc as well.

Its API is nowhere near complete as GNU-EFI's or EDKII's, so it provides seamless integration with those headers to make the API expandable. It is also not a fully POSIX standard compatible libc, it's just a wrapper around the firmware provided features with some minimal additions, but provides enough for everyday use cases. As being minimal, it's extremely small (~132K of source only) and because it's dependency-free, it's easy to integrate into any project.

The repo contains lots of examples too, from a simple "Hello World" to more complex ones like displaying a PNG splash screen or loading a "kernel" in ELF format.

POSIX-UEFI is 100% AI-free, and has been tested on almost every VMs and on lots of real hardware by volunteers over the years. It is feature complete, stable and considered bug-free by now (big thanks to contributors), although some workarounds for buggy firmware might be added in the future.

story_text.value:
Source code: http://github.com/shawwn/sharc

I had more things I wanted to do with this, but I should probably admit to myself I probably won't be.

The original idea was for https://news.ycombinator.lol to be "Hacker News, but all the comments are AI." Right now it's "Hacker News, but all the comments are the same as the real HN." Hence, it's completely pointless.

Special thanks to dang for collaborating -- he even suggested the name for the codebase, "sharc".

Development time was about four months of near daily work: https://github.com/shawwn/sharc/tree/main/docs/agents/handof... Some days I'd spend a solid 16 hours on this.

What's the point? None, really. Just to test the limits of my abilities and prove to myself that I could do what pg did.

It's an extremely efficient port of HN to Common Lisp. One of the project's goals was to be high performance. According to benchmarks, it can generate pages very slightly slower than real HN. (dang shared some timings on a particularly busy page, along with how many views it got over a certain time period, for benchmarking throughput. I never got around to verifying whether I can handle 24 million views a day, though, so I'd imagine something might break if you scale this up. On the other hand, I think it'll hold up.)

If you're particularly offended that this is copying your comments, claim your account by going to your profile (for example, I would go to https://news.ycombinator.lol/user?id=sillysaurusx) and then click "claim" at the bottom. It'll ask you to put a 6 digit code into your real HN profile, at which point you'll be able to reset your cloned profile's password. Log in, go to your profile page, and set "redact" to "yes", the same way you'd set "showdead" to "yes" on HN.

So, why make this? Eh, call it an art project. That's code for "It would've been a lot funnier with AI generated comments, but I seem to have stopped working on this for now." I'll post an update someday, if I can figure out how to do it without paying hundreds of dollars of API token prices.

/ask and /show are missing. Those were the only two features left to clone. But pretty much everything else is there. It's been running for a couple months now, so I suppose it's stable enough for a public showing.

Not that there's any reason to look. Shoo! Go find a more worthy project to devote your attention to. :)

Kind of melancholy admitting that I spent four months with only something pointless to show for it.

But then again, here's the punchline: go to any random comment on HN, then in the url change .com to .lol and you'll see an almost pixel perfect recreation. For example, https://news.ycombinator.lol/item?id=49995615

Sadly you can't form a loop, because if you edit your original comment with a link to itself, you'd only be able to go from HN to .lol to HN. But you could list both and switch between them as much as you want.

For example:

https://news.ycombinator.lol/item?id=49996495

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49996495

This project was one of the most technically demanding things I've ever done. People look at HN and go oh, that? That looks easy. If you think so, I invite you to write it yourself -- it's an exercise that'll certainly make you a better programmer, and gain appreciation for how many subtle features we enjoy here on HN.

Ha, and I just discovered a new one. I mixed up the "title" and "url" boxes just now. HN popped up a nice looking overlay that said "please enter a URL", pointing to the actual url box. https://i.imgur.com/agFas7x.png The HN team is always adding something or another, even if it's not always visible. Normally I'd dive into this and find out how it works and clone it, but ... eh, I'll settle for a 95% exact clone.

story_text.value:
Going to some shady website for file conversions was really annoying me because I had to hope whatever I gave them wasn't saved, and whatever I got back wasn't something "unexpected." So I made convkit, a CLI that does file conversions 100% locally. Run

    conv in.mp4 out.gif
and you get your GIF from the right tool (ffmpeg, ImageMagick, etc.) using settings tuned for good output. For example, a GIF's 256 colors are picked from the clip itself instead of ffmpeg's generic palette.

And if you've ever had an issue uploading a file that is too large, you can use the --max-size flag:

    conv clip.mp4 --max-size 10mb
It trades resolution, frame rate and bitrate against each other, so you get the best-looking version that still fits.

Notes

- In early stages (0.3.x) so some issues pop up

- You only need the tools for the conversions you use, so video and GIFs only need ffmpeg; LibreOffice, pandoc and Typst are only for documents; Image to Image needs ImageMagick.

- Not all features are listed. If you are interested go to the github page! https://github.com/shdwfruit/convkit

- If you want any specific conversions, let me know!

Thanks for reading!

story_text.value:
I built FunFrame so my kids could play with our family photos without me hovering over the Photos app. It turns pictures from your library into jigsaw puzzles and Memory Match, plus a gallery a two-year-old can't edit, delete, or share from.

A few things HN might find interesting:

- There's no server. No accounts, no analytics, no third-party SDKs, and no network code of its own. The only traffic iOS attributes to the app is iCloud Photos downloading your own pictures so they can be shown.

- Pieces are cut on device with bezier knobs seeded by grid position, so neighbors always interlock. The grid follows the photo's shape, so a wide photo gets a wide board of near-square pieces. SpriteKit for the board, SwiftUI for the rest, SQLite through the C API, no dependencies.

- Every finger holds its own piece, so two kids can work one puzzle at the same time.

- Settings sit behind a math question. I shipped a switch to turn it off on my own devices, and App Review rejected the release under guideline 1.3: in the Kids category the gate can't be optional. Guided Access is the supported answer.

- The only machine learning is on-device face detection, used to center the double-tap zoom. Nothing is stored.

It's free, with no ads and nothing to buy. iPad first, and it runs on iPhone. I'd especially like to hear from parents of 2 to 5 year olds about what's confusing or missing.

story_text.value:
I struggle with the way Claude speaks to me when I do work. So much text, every, single, time.

When I ask a question, I get an essay back, and with so many weird constructs: slogans, metaphors, recaps, strange choice of nouns, "it's not X, it's Y".

Claude's own "concise" mode shortens it, somewhat, but keeps the the rest of the slop.

I tried system prompts, those got forgotten after a couple of turns. I tried looking for plugins but none consistently made Claude speak normally. Some where slash commands, other solved for token use, others solved for neurodivergence.

I just wanted to not read an essay and make Claude get to the point fast, every single time.

Is that so much to ask? Apparently; it took me weeks of trial and error to make something that worked for me, I have stories, but I'm sharing it as a claude code plugin with you, those of you who struggle with Claude, the same way I did.

title.value: Show HN: Terse, a Claude Code plugin that halves reply length by cutting filler

story_text.value:
Hi, I'm a former SDET and now solo dev of VoiceGremlin, a tool for automated tests against AI that answer phones. You pass the API a phone number and a test case like "Verify that the agent does X." It calls your voice agent, tests the thing by having the bots talk to each other, and uses LLM-as-judge to provide a pass/fail for your pipeline.

State: Fully working, free trial, no card needed. Try it out and please give me feedback, especially if you run in to problems.

Goal: I built VoiceGremlin with the explicit goal of being Mailosaur for phone agents. We paid for Mailosaur at work because the alternative (having our automated tests interact programmatically with our corporate Outlook server) was doable, but very painful, both technically and organizationally. The lesson I learned was "doable, but painful" is a good sign of a SaaS opportunity.

Well, getting an automated test to call a phone number is also painful. Telephony providers are tough to get onboarded as vendors. Using your own STT/TTS means a lot of bandwidth moving through wherever you run your test automation from. It's tricky to get the LLM-to-LLM prompts dialed in enough to avoid flaky tests. Etc.

Process: It took about 45 days to build, with half of that being businessy stuff like implementing Stripe and my feeble attempts at marketing, and the other half being experimenting with different telephony providers and features, testing different models, prompt tweaking, and fraud/abuse prevention.

Design goal: Do one thing, do it well, and get out of the way. There's no ambition to manage your test cases for you, host your voice agents, or add upsell features.

Stack: The dependencies are Supabase (DB and authentication), Netlify (static storage and API routing), Digitalocean (the server component that makes the calls), Telnyx (easier to work with than Twilio IMO), Stripe, Openrouter, Cloudflare (captcha on signup). Oh, and I host my private git in Keybase, the greatest tool nobody uses.

Thanks!

My biggest issue with Jellyfin was always the UI, so I rebuilt Plex Web on top of it. It runs in the browser and connects to your existing Jellyfin server.

story_text.value:
Hi HN. I'm Hunter, one of the co-founders of Daydream, a small music research lab.

Our research focus is musical control. Musicians steer each other by a shared set of rules: the chart, the groove, who's carrying the melody. We are building control models with real-time performance and an actual understanding of music.

Our core real-time engine is open source and can be found here: https://github.com/daydreamlive/DEMON

The preview I'm sharing is an in-browser recording studio with virtual session players you can direct in real time. You record, upload, or generate a source track. Then you book "session players" and build your way to a full song.

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I’m Louis, Co-Founder of Armature (YC P26), where we help teams make their product discoverable and usable by coding agents. We already measured 50k+ agent sessions and realized that over and over agents would encounter the exact same limitations on different tasks using the same tool. So we wondered why these weren’t fixed. And the answer is simple: the feedback loop just doesn’t exist between agents and software vendors but also between different agents. Humans can share their experience on platforms like https://g2.com and https://trustpilot.com, but agents have nowhere to.

So we created: https://agent.reviews: the G2 for agents.

It works with a set of skills and an npm CLI (@armature-tech/agent-reviews) connecting agents to our API endpoints. Anyone can ask their agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.) to install it, and agents will naturally check reviews before picking a tool and post their own after using one.

As usual, privacy was our main concern, so we added 3 layers before a review gets posted: Deterministic rules filtering secrets, PII, URLs, etc. A Jev classifier trained to detect any leak after the first check A small LLM checking each review to make sure nothing was missed

We've been sharing this project around for a few weeks now and gathered thousands of reviews already. There are already interesting ones, for example:

- A Claude Code agent noticed that the Stripe SDK systematically crashed when the API key was missing on the health check page (while it’s this page’s role to actually return an “API key missing” error)

- 2 agents mentioned that Prisma required a DATABASE_URL variable even when it wasn’t connecting to any database. They both put fake URLs as a workaround, and it worked.

We truly think the agent experience needs the same community effect user experience has, so everyone benefits from it: agents can pick the tools that are best optimized for them and software companies can improve their product based on real feedback. That’s why we made sure accessing reviews is free for both humans and agents and just requires copy/pasting one prompt for the agent to install our CLI & skill, start the authentication flow, and submit their first review (this helps us prevent unauthorized scraping and spam reviews).

Would you let your agents submit and read reviews too? We’d love for you to set up agent reviews, ask your agent to check reviews next time it needs to pick a tool and post its own experience when using it. Then tell us how it went!

title.value: Show HN: Agent.reviews – Where AI agents read and write reviews on tools

story_text.value:
akicode is a coding app for kids that runs and single-steps Python and C++ entirely in your browser. No server or account needed.

Underneath is a Linux clone written in TypeScript, and real Linux programs run on it unmodified, including gdb behind the Debug button.

Just for fun, you can also open the Linux terminal: xeyes and xcalc open real X11 windows, and there is even a redis-server/redis-cli, just because it works.

title.value: Show HN: A Linux clone in TypeScript, hidden in an IDE for kids
